title: Keep one story of Rumi
hookLine: longing, the beloved, the Prophet, the Quran, being cooked

cards: A reed crying. A parrot playing dead. A lion leaping at his own face in a well.

Yesterday's keepsake was one line of the emperor; Rumi's Masnavi hands over pictures instead. That's how Rumi taught: a story, then another story tucked inside it, then a turn toward God, then back to the story.
The stories are how his teaching travels from one person to the next. So today, not a quotation: keep one story of Rumi.

teach.h: THE REED, THE PHYSICIAN, THE PARROTS.
teach.b: Walk back through the stories. The reed flute, cut from the reedbed, crying to go home: longing as a direction.

The king and the handmaid, and the physician who found the real cause of her sickness when her pulse leapt at the name Samarkand. The grocer's parrot, who decided every bald man must have spilled oil too.

teach.h: THE LION, THE HARPER, THE SHEPHERD.
teach.b: The lion and the hare, where the animals say trust God and the lion says effort is God's way too, echoing the saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, about trusting God and still tying your camel.
The merchant's parrot, who played dead and flew free. The old harper, playing for God alone in a graveyard, found and seen by the caliph Umar.
Moses and the shepherd, and the voice that told Moses he was sent to join people to God, not to part them. The elephant in the dark, each hand touching only part.

teach.h: THE CHICKPEA, THE MIRROR, THE DOOR.
teach.b: The chickpea in the boiling pot, told the heat is making it good. The Chinese and Greek painters, and the wall polished into a mirror. The lover at the door who learned to say it is you.
The guest house. Ayaz and his old shoes. Now the threads.
Longing: we're all parted from our source. The beloved: God, and the friend through whom God showed up.
The Prophet and the Quran: story after story leans on a verse or a saying, and tradition says the poet Jami called the Masnavi the Quran in the Persian tongue.
And being cooked: a saying often attributed to Rumi sums up his life as raw, then cooked, then burned.
Every story is heat doing its work.

how: In Persian-speaking and Turkish Sufi circles, the Masnavi is read aloud and explained story by story, often in weekly gatherings, and its tales are retold in homes and sermons.

o: a prayer book used for daily Muslim worship
a Persian epic of kings and ancient heroes

games.q: a friend asks what Rumi is actually about. you have one minute. what do you do?
o: tell one story, beginning, middle and turn.
games.why: Rumi taught through stories, and the Masnavi travels that way: a reed, a parrot, a chickpea, each turning toward God.

practice: Let the stories drift past, the reed, the parrot, the lion in the well, the chickpea, and wait for the one that won't leave. Tell it inside, in your own words, beginning, middle and turn, as if to a child at bedtime.

wordCard.voice: Masnavi, Rumi's book of stories: the reed, the parrot, the chickpea, each one teaching through a story instead of a lecture. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: keep one story. A story only lives if it's told. That's day two hundred twenty-six.
